rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Ion pumps move ions **uphill**, and the syllabus names two machines. The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is **primary** active transport: one ATP buys **3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in**, maintaining the ≈ −70 mV resting potential, cell volume, and the Na⁺ gradient everything else feeds on.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Na⁺/K⁺ pump: 3 Na⁺ (out) + 2 K⁺ (in) per ATP hydrolysed - Resting membrane potential ≈ −70 mV (maintained by the pump) - Na⁺–glucose symport: Na⁺ (down gradient) + glucose (up gradient), same direction

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Covers only: ion pumps, sodium-potassium, sodium-glucose pump (within Bio-inorganic Chemistry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses one ATP to transport three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell, both against their concentration gradients."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***ORS in a cholera ward*** — sugar and salt in the right proportions keep the SGLT symporter loaded, so the gut keeps absorbing water precisely when its passive absorption has failed; the pump mechanism saves millions of lives a year.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Body's Electricity Bill Ion pumps are the molecular machines that move ions **against** their concentration gradients, spending ATP to do it. The syllabus names two: the **sodium–potassium pump** (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase), which keeps nerves liveable, and the **sodium–glucose pump**, which uses the sodium gradient as a battery to absorb glucose.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Passive versus active transport - **Passive transport (diffusion):** particles move **down** their concentration gradient; no energy spent. Ions need a channel/protein, but the gradient does the work.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Numbers: 3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in per ATP; resting potential ~ -70 mV. Na+-glucose = symport = secondary active; Na+/K+ = primary active (ATPase). ORS = glucose + Na+ co-transport.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the sodium–potassium pump, its stoichiometry and its importance.** — The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is a membrane enzyme that hydrolyses ATP and uses the energy to move ions **against** their gradients: **3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Explain the sodium–glucose pump in the intestine. Why is it called secondary active transport?** — In the intestinal lining, a symporter protein (**SGLT**) binds **Na⁺ and glucose on the same side** of the membrane and carries both **in the same direction** into the cell.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always label which pump is primary (Na+/K+ ATPase) and which is secondary (Na+-glucose symport) — the classification itself carries marks even when the mechanism is described correctly.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: One gradient spends, one gradient earns: the sodium-glucose pump is a chain in which Na+ falling down the gradient the Na+/K+ pump built pays for glucose climbing its own — secondary active transport in one sentence.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Passive transport = down gradient, no energy; active transport = against gradient, needs energy. Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+ ATPase, primary active): 3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in per ATP; maintains resting potential (~ -70 mV), cell volume, and the Na+ gradient; runs constantly because ions leak.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The Na+/K+ pump is among the body's largest ATP consumers — in resting humans a large fraction of basal metabolism goes to it, with the brain's share the highest of any organ.

rows.text: Explain how the sodium-glucose pump absorbs glucose against its gradient and why ORS contains both sugar and salt.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **The sodium–glucose pump does not split ATP:** its direct energy is the Na⁺ gradient; the ATP was spent upstream by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Calling it "ATP-driven" without the intermediate loses the mechanism mark.  ·  **3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in — not the reverse:** the pump exports more than it imports (which is why it is electrogenic), but the counts are 3 out, 2 in.
